Neonatal Caribbean sharpnose sharks (Rhizoprionodon porosus) are born at approximately 35 cm [Lb = approximately 35 cm] in total length, a measurement based on field captures of near-term gravid females and verified through size-frequency analysis of neonates caught in nursery grounds along the northern coast of South America. Litter sizes reported for this species are modest, typically ranging from 2 to 6 pups per litter [N_R_i = 2 to 6 pups per litter], and reproductive females are thought to produce a single litter each year [F_R_i = single litter each year], a breeding frequency that aligns with the energetic constraints of viviparous elasmobranchs in warm, productive coastal waters. The gestation period itself is influenced by ambient environmental conditions; under the thermal regime characteristic of these tropical habitats, with a mean water temperature of 24.2 °C [T = 24.2 °C], the age at birth has been estimated at 270 days [ab = 270 days]. This relatively protracted development reflects the reliance on yolk reserves supplemented by histotrophic secretions during the later stages of embryogenesis, a pattern common among carcharhinid sharks.

Females of the Caribbean sharpnose shark ultimately attain a considerably larger body size than males, with the greatest total length recorded for adult females reaching 113 cm [Li = 113 cm]. This sexual dimorphism in maximum body length is a well-documented feature within the genus Rhizoprionodon and is typically attributed to the selective pressures associated with fecundity, as larger females can accommodate more developing embryos and produce larger litters. The ultimate wet weight corresponding to this asymptotic length has been estimated at 4.7 kilograms [Wwi = 4.7 kilograms], a relationship derived from length-weight regressions applied to a substantial sample of mature individuals from populations in the western Atlantic. These large females are reproductively active for numerous years, contributing multiple cohorts of pups to the population over their lifetime.

The onset of sexual maturity in female Caribbean sharpnose sharks occurs when individuals attain a total length of approximately 65 cm [Lp = approximately 65 cm]. This length at puberty represents a critical life-history transition, marking the point at which individuals shift from a growth-dominated phase toward reproductive investment, specifically the maturation of ovarian follicles and the onset of vitellogenesis. Field studies examining the reproductive tracts of females captured across the species' range have consistently identified the 65 cm threshold as the point at which the majority of individuals exhibit signs of recent or impending ovulation. The total length at puberty for both sexes is also closely tied to geographic location; populations inhabiting cooler or less productive waters may delay the onset of maturity until slightly larger sizes are attained, although the 65 cm value remains a robust benchmark for the species as a whole, particularly in the well-studied Brazilian and Caribbean stocks.

Under the stable thermal conditions typical of its tropical and subtropical distribution, where water temperatures hover near an annual mean of 24.2 °C [T = 24.2 °C], the Caribbean sharpnose shark exhibits a maximum lifespan of approximately 8 years [am = approximately 8 years]. This longevity is intermediate among carcharhinid sharks of comparable body size and is thought to be constrained by high rates of natural mortality experienced by juveniles and sub-adults in coastal nursery habitats subject to intense predation pressure from larger piscivores. Age determination analyses based on vertebral band counts have confirmed that the 8-year lifespan is reached by a small number of individuals, with most adults surviving only 5 to 6 years. The species' relatively rapid life history, characterized by early maturation and moderate longevity, makes it resilient to moderate fishing pressure in some regions, though population declines have been documented in areas where artisanal gillnet fisheries are intensive.

The reproductive biology of the Caribbean sharpnose shark is further characterized by the maximum reproductive capacity, which integrates typical fecundity and breeding frequency. Under the favorable thermal environment of 24.2 °C [T = 24.2 °C], the maximum reproductive rate equates to approximately 4 pups per year per female. This annual output of a single, moderately sized litter is relatively modest compared to that of some other small coastal sharks, where biennial or triennial reproductive cycles impose even lower lifetime fecundity. The species' strategy is consistent with the energetic demands of viviparity and the need to allocate resources toward both gestation and post-parturition recovery in a seasonally variable environment. Comparing this pattern to other carcharhiniform sharks of similar size reveals a continuum from annual reproduction in warmer waters to less frequent breeding at higher latitudes, a gradient that shapes population dynamics across the species' geographic range.
